Hoffman, 49, was originally charged with first-degree felony continuous sexual abuse of a child, involving his son's friend between 2019 and 2022. The original charges carried a potential maximum sentence of life in prison without parole. [1, 2, 3]
In June 2025, his initial trial ended in a mistrial due to a 7-5 hung jury. Following the mistrial, prosecutors from the Texas Office of the Attorney General (OAG) stated that the victim declined to testify a second time to avoid further trauma, which prompted them to seek a plea agreement. [1, 2, 3]
The Plea Deal Terms
Under the terms negotiated by the OAG and accepted in April 2026, the felony charges were significantly reduced: [1, 2]
Reduced Charges: Hoffman pleaded guilty to two Class A misdemeanors: indecent assault and displaying harmful material to a minor. [1, 2]
No Sex Offender Registration: The OAG deal explicitly waived the requirement for Hoffman to register as a sex offender within the state of Texas (though he subsequently registered in Nebraska where he relocated). [1, 2]
Law License Forfeiture: Hoffman was required to resign his Texas law license for a minimum of five years. His resignation was formally accepted by the Texas Supreme Court, preventing him from practicing law. [1, 2, 3]
Protective Order: A lifetime protective order was issued, banning any future contact with the victim. [1, 2]
Sentencing and Intervention
The leniency of the initial plea agreement caused widespread public outrage. The OAG prosecutors originally presented a deal that would have required Hoffman to serve minimal to no jail time (with critics noting the office originally sought as little as a single day in prison). [1, 2]
Visiting Judge Roy Sparkman heavily criticized the arrangement. Rejecting the initial timeline, Judge Sparkman doubled the proposed 30-day jail term to a 60-day sentence. Hoffman began serving his sentence on April 27, 2026, but was released early after serving 29 days due to standard credit for good behavior. During the emotional sentencing hearing, the victim's mother provided an impact statement and offered Hoffman a Bible, stating she agreed to the plea deal solely to protect her child from the witness stand. 8 Lessons from Shipping 2,500 PRs a Month: Rethinking AI Agent Architecture - Scaling Agent Trust and Velocity at SpaceX

Introduction: The Agent Micromanagement Trap

Many modern software engineers integrating AI into their workflows quickly hit an frustrating operational ceiling: spending hours manually micromanaging a single agent chat window or acting as a human "meat proxy" between disconnected tools. In the early days of AI-assisted coding, developers sat bound to terminal orchestrators, manually copying context, pasting error logs, and babysitting individual prompts.

To break through this velocity bottleneck, engineering systems must fundamentally evolve. Poteto—creator of the pstack skill library and engineer at Cursor and SpaceX AI—realized this friction firsthand while optimizing severe performance issues in Cursor's laggy agents window. As a former engineer on Meta’s React team, she found herself manually serving as an inefficient bridge between AI agents and Chrome DevTools flame graphs or heap snapshots.

Scaling development output from a handful of manual pull requests to thousands per month requires abandoning unguided "vibe coding" and chat babysitting. Instead, engineers must focus on building rigorous environmental constraints, automated inner- and outer-loop feedback systems, and specialized agent topologies. Here are eight architectural lessons derived from shipping 2,500 pull requests a month to production.

1. Ditch the "Factory"—Manage a "Michelin Kitchen" Instead

While Andrej Karpathy popularized the concept of "vibe coding"—a high-level paradigm where "the code almost doesn't exist" to the developer—Poteto offers a contrasting operational framework: the Michelin Kitchen.

The software factory metaphor often conjures images of cold, mechanical, mass-produced output where quality takes a back seat to raw volume. In contrast, the Michelin Kitchen framework treats software creation as a disciplined craft centered on environment design, precise tooling, and operational topology. In this framework, the software engineer shifts from a line worker to an executive chef:

   - Executive Chef (The Software Engineer): Designs the overall environment, sharpens tooling, establishes strict guardrails, organizes kitchen workflows, and maintains total accountability for final production quality.

   - Sous Chefs (The AI Agents): Autonomous execution agents assigned to specific stations that handle prep work, feature implementation, and verification within defined operational boundaries.

"as a chef you're in a position where you're not necessarily cooking all the food yourself anymore but you are thinking... like the tech lead for the kitchen where chefs have to think about not just cooking but they have to basically organize the whole kitchen"

Engineers scale development velocity not by abandoning code craft or ignoring codebase mechanics, but by scaling domain expertise and intent through structured, operational kitchen processes.

2. Constrain the Environment, Not the Model

A fundamental reality of working with frontier AI models is that poor codebase environments lead directly to "garbage in, garbage out" results. Trying to fix flawed agent output solely by prompting harder in a chat window yields diminishing returns; true architectural leverage lies in environmental design.

A helpful mental model for constraint design is type narrowing in TypeScript—where a broad, ambiguous type is systematically narrowed through type guards into a specific, controlled type. Environmental constraints narrow the decision space for agents in the exact same manner.

To enforce this, SpaceX AI and Cursor utilize an internal framework called Dune for their Electron applications. Acting like an "internal Next.js for our Electron apps," Dune enforces strict boundaries:

   - Restrictive Lint Rules: The framework enforces strict linting rules that explicitly block agents from introducing anti-patterns or taking unapproved shortcuts.

   - Conventional Directory Architectures: Features must reside in dedicated feature directories discovered via an automated registry pattern.

   - Preventing "God Files": Early iterations of internal tools like Grockbot suffered from monolithic 10,000-line "god files." Structural directory rules prevent agents from continuously appending code to giant files, forcing clean modularity.

When an agent makes a mistake, the human engineer's response should not be to yell at the chat window. Instead, that failure should be converted into a permanent lint rule, structural directory constraint, or type-narrowing logic within the codebase environment.

3. Offload Determinism to Custom CLIs to Save Your Context Window

Engineering workflows naturally fall along a spectrum ranging from Non-Deterministic Judgment (architectural intent, design tradeoffs, high-level reasoning) to Deterministic Mechanics (AST code transformations, code refactoring, running test suites).

As frontier models become significantly more capable, skill definitions must evolve. Older skill setups heavily spelled out explicit CLI command lists and low-level syntax instructions. Frontier models already know how to execute standard syntax independently; spelling out mechanical steps wastes precious context window capacity.

To maximize execution speed and conserve tokens for complex reasoning, deterministic operations should be offloaded into custom executable scripts and CLI wrappers inside skill directories:

   - Preserving Context Window Capacity: Wrapping deterministic tasks (such as interacting with Playwright or Chrome DevTools Protocol) in lightweight CLI scripts keeps Markdown instructions lightweight. This leaves the model's context window dedicated strictly to non-deterministic judgment.

   - Preventing "Rebuilding the World": Without CLI wrappers, agents tend to rewrite and test execution scripts from scratch every session, wasting tokens and introducing erratic execution behavior.

   - Compressing Intent: Concise natural language skill files act as compressed process maps, defining human intent and guardrails while delegating heavy mechanical labor to executable code wrappers.

4. Connect Outer-Loop Triggers to Inner-Loop "Chiefs of Staff"

Scaling high-volume software delivery requires seamlessly bridging two distinct automation loops without requiring human "meat proxies" to manually copy-paste context:

   A. The Outer Loop: Driven by connectors like Grockbot running background watching routines across external platforms (Slack, Linear, email, X) to aggregate incoming bug reports and system performance feedback.

   B. The Inner Loop: Managed inside cloud-based environments like Cursor Projects, where cloud-based coordinator agents operate on dedicated compute infrastructure as "chiefs of staff" or executive chefs.

Grockbot bridges these loops via direct APIs, transmitting individual or batched context payloads (such as 30 performance bug reports simultaneously) directly into Cursor Projects without human intervention.

Crucially, the inner-loop chief-of-staff agent ingests the payload, evaluates task topologies, and delegates work to sub-agents while maintaining centralized threading across all incoming tasks. Without a coordinator maintaining centralized context, isolated sub-agents act in silos—resulting in duplicated code changes across identical files and failing to spot the overarching root cause behind related bug reports.

5. Deploy Verifier Swarms to Turn "One-Way Doors" into "Two-Way Doors"

In autonomous workflows, software changes fall into two distinct risk profiles:

   - One-Way Doors: Irreversible, high-risk changes (e.g., schema migrations causing data loss, severe security vulnerabilities).

   - Two-Way Doors: Safe, easily reversible code changes that can be merged and quickly rolled back if issues arise.

Programmatic verifiability turns high-risk changes into safe, reversible "two-way doors." This enables algorithmic hill climbing, where agents continuously execute changes, measure output against a quantitative scoring rubric or benchmark, and autonomously iterate in a closed feedback loop. For example, Poteto applied hill climbing to optimize Cursor's laggy agents window, enabling agents to autonomously diagnose and repair performance bottlenecks using runtime heap snapshots and flame graphs.

When engaging Full Autopilot mode in PAC (Poteto Agent Architecture), the system spawns a dedicated verifier swarm (up to 10 agents per PR):

   - Runtime UI Fuzzing: Verifier agents run custom CLIs wrapping Playwright and Chrome DevTools Protocol to spin up the actual application, click through the interface like a human user, and systematically hunt for edge-case bugs and performance regressions.

   - Self-Correcting Repair Loops: If fuzzing surfaces a regression, verifiers independently apply repairs, re-run tests, and hill-climb until all checks pass cleanly, enabling safe overnight autonomous merging.

"verification... is probably the most important skill in PAC... because without verification... if the agent can't actually see the result of its work there's no way it can actually iterate"

6. Stop Gating Every Pull Request—Switch to "Quality Sampling"

Human engineers cannot manually review 2,500 pull requests a month. Attempting to gate every individual change creates an immediate operational bottleneck. To scale output, engineers must transition from pre-merge gatekeeping to post-facto quality sampling.

Under this paradigm, full-autopilot verifier swarms test, repair, and merge code continuously (such as during overnight dark-factory runs). The following morning, the engineer assumes the role of a factory quality supervisor:

   A. Post-Facto Auditing: The engineer audits merged commits from the repository log post-merge rather than blocking individual PRs pre-merge.

   B. Pattern Extraction: When bad patterns, shortcuts, or propagated workarounds are identified in merged code, the engineer steps back to evaluate the systemic cause.

   C. Environment Course Correction: The recurring flaw is converted into a permanent lint rule, structural directory constraint, or updated skill definition to systematically prevent the failure from reoccurring.

"as a quality supervisor on a factory you can't look at every single item you sample... you look at the quality of the pull requests you look at the code that the agents are writing and you scrutinize it very rigorously... and then you think about how to course correct the environment"

7. Build a "Recall Engine" to Mine Past Chat Transcripts

Historical agent chat transcripts represent a materialized, real-world record of problem-solving processes. Instead of allowing past session logs to sit idle, developers can use a recall engine (such as the recall skill in Pstack) to mine transcripts and extract reusable workflow skills.

The recall process converts past manual corrections into automated operational guardrails:

   A. Transcript Analysis: Scans historical logs to locate exact moments where a developer intervened, supplied missing context, or corrected an agent's reasoning—such as when Poteto repeatedly intervened while debugging complex React virtualization issues within the Cursor application itself.

   B. Logic Extraction: Extracts the underlying human domain expertise, decision frameworks, and guardrails behind the developer's manual prompt corrections.

   C. Process Compression: Collapses those instructions into compact Markdown skill files, shifting skills away from low-level syntax manuals toward compressed workflow maps.

   D. Workflow Synthesis: Combines intent-refining skills (such as Matt Pocock's grill me or wayfinder) with execution skills (such as Pstack's poteto mode) to curate a personalized developer "knife set."

Encoding past interventions directly into reusable skill files ensures future agents automatically adhere to proven workflows, preventing repeated errors without requiring manual micromanagement.

8. Implement "Gardening Routines" to Avoid Pure Execution Mode

To maintain codebase health without overwhelming technical leads, background gardening routines continuously scan repositories for anti-patterns, deprecated syntax, or known framework foot guns (e.g., common React anti-patterns).

However, a critical tactical rule governs these routines: Do not immediately spawn sub-agents to fix issues as soon as they are flagged.

Instead, background agents append detected flaws to a centralized queue document.

Creating a buffered queue prevents engineers and chief-of-staff agents from falling into a reactive "pure execution mode." By reviewing the queued buffer document every few days, engineers can analyze systemic code smells across the entire repository, identify root causes, and resolve flaws in batches via automated codemods or structural lint rules.

Conclusion: The Changing Role of Domain Expertise

Scaling software delivery velocity to thousands of monthly pull requests relies on ascending the Agent Trust Ladder. Developers climb this ladder not through blind faith in model capabilities, but by earning trust through sharp codebase environments, rigorous programmatic verification loops, and compressed natural language process maps.

Far from rendering technical knowledge obsolete, domain expertise is more critical now than ever. As frontier models handle mechanical syntax generation, the primary bottleneck in software creation shifts entirely to articulating precise human intent, establishing domain guardrails, and designing systemic environments.

As automated kitchens take over mechanical execution and dark-factory workflows handle routine maintenance, every software architect must ask: Are you spending your day micromanaging individual tasks, or are you stepping up to design the kitchen?

April 6, 1967. Seaman Apprentice Doug Hegdahl, 20 years old, a farm kid from South Dakota, is on deck of the cruiser USS Canberra in the Gulf of Tonkin at night when a 5-inch gun fires.

The blast knocks him overboard.

He treads water for hours until Vietnamese fishermen pull him out. He ends up in the Hanoi Hilton.

His interrogators can't believe a sailor just fell off a ship, so they assume he's a commando. Hegdahl figures out his best chance is to act dumb. He plays the bumpkin. He pretends he can't read or write. They assign a guard to teach him. He never learns.

They give up and nickname him "The Incredibly Stupid One." Then they let him wander the camp almost freely.

It was the worst mistake they ever made with him.

With an Air Force officer coaching him, Hegdahl memorized the names, capture dates and personal details of about 256 fellow prisoners. He locked them in his head by singing them to the tune of "Old MacDonald Had a Farm," over and over.

He talked the guards into taking him into Hanoi for new glasses and memorized the route. He also put dirt in the fuel tanks of five North Vietnamese trucks.

The POWs had a rule: nobody accepts early release. They made one exception. When Hanoi offered to free Hegdahl for propaganda in 1969, his senior officer ordered him to go.

He walked out with 256 names in his head. For hundreds of families, it was the first proof their men were alive.

The North Vietnamese had sent home the most dangerous man in the camp.

A tax-exempt hospital quoted a nun $80,000 for a joint replacement Medicare pays about $16,000 for. Five times Medicare. Her offense was asking for a fair price.

Katy Talento, a former White House health policy advisor who now runs a health plan for a community of nuns, laid out the whole story this week. The sister is in severe pain, has no income, and gets her care paid for by donors. Her plan offered the hospital cash, up front, bundled, at 125% of Medicare. The hospital countered at 250%. When they explained she'd qualify for Medicaid and for the hospital's own charity program, the price doubled again.

Federal law makes the irony worse. Under Section 501(r), if she'd come in uninsured and applied for financial assistance, the hospital couldn't charge her more than what it generally bills insured patients, a number it can peg to Medicare. A charity case gets protected. A plan offering cash above Medicare gets the spite price. Her surgeon was horrified and is now personally pushing the hospital to accept $30,000.

Now the numbers behind the "charity" label, all cited in her piece.

Nonprofit hospitals received about $37.4 billion in tax breaks in 2021, per a JAMA study led by Johns Hopkins economist Ge Bai. $11.5 billion in federal income tax, $9.1 billion in sales tax, $7.8 billion in property tax. They provided $15.2 billion in charity care. That's 41 cents per dollar of tax break.

The largest 7% of nonprofit hospitals collected as much in tax breaks as the other 93% combined. By 2022 nonprofit hospitals held $447 billion in investment assets, and the richest 1% held 42% of it.

Per $100 of expenses, nonprofits spend about $2.30 on charity care. For-profit hospitals, which pay taxes, spend $3.80. Government hospitals spend $4.10.

The Lown Institute found 54% of nonprofit hospitals in a 20-state analysis fall short of the value of their tax breaks, by a combined $11.5 billion a year. GAO found 30 hospitals that reported spending nothing at all on community benefit in 2016.

Here's why. 501(r) requires a financial assistance policy and a community needs report every three years. It sets no minimum amount of charity. The first hospital ever stripped of its exemption under it lost status for failing to publish the report.

And when a for-profit hospital converts to nonprofit, a new Georgia State study of 150 conversions found charity care didn't meaningfully rise, while local school districts lost about $25 per resident in property tax.

Meanwhile Providence, one of the biggest Catholic systems, hired McKinsey to build a revenue program, and Washington's attorney general got $157.8 million in refunds and debt relief for nearly 100,000 patients.

Cash up front should be every provider's favorite customer. This hospital punished it.

text:
A seventeen-year-old boy stepped on his own daddy's hand in the dark. He had been trying to start his father's truck, and his father was lying underneath it by the gate, a few hours before the two of them were supposed to leave Mississippi for good. When the sheriff came out that night he went through the dead man's wallet, right there in front of the boy, and he took something out of it.

It was going on eleven o'clock on the night of Friday, January 31, 1964, and Hank Allen was seventeen years old and driving home from a party in Gloster.

His cousin John Horton was in the passenger seat, sixteen. The car was a 1954 DeSoto and the road was Highway 24, running east toward Liberty, Mississippi.

Hank made the left into his family's driveway and drove up toward the gap.

That was what they called the gate his father had built into the barbed wire, the one that kept the chickens and the mules from wandering off the place. His father's bobtailed Ford logging truck was sitting just outside it, engine off, headlights burning.

Hank could not think why his daddy would leave the truck across the driveway like that.

He got out and called for him. Nothing came back, so he walked around the truck and climbed up into the cab and turned the key, thinking maybe the battery had gone flat and his father had walked up to the house for help.

The battery had gone flat.

He climbed back down, and coming off the running board his foot came down on something in the dark that was not ground.

It was his father's right hand.

Hank backed the DeSoto up and put the headlights under the truck. Louis Allen was lying face down beside his own front gate, forty-four years old, and he had been dead for a little while.

The boy went to reach for him. John caught his arm and would not let go, because John understood something Hank was not able to think about yet, which was that in Amite County a Black boy did not touch a body before the white law had seen it.

So they got back in the car and drove two miles east to the sheriff's house.

They got there near midnight. As Hank came up on Sheriff Daniel Jones's back door he heard a sound he knew, the sound of a shotgun being pumped somewhere inside.

He knocked anyway and told the sheriff that somebody had shot his father.

"Is he dead?" Jones asked him.

Hank said he hoped not. Walking back to his car he heard the shotgun pump a second time.

Here is who was lying under that truck.

Louis Allen was born in Amite County in April of 1919 and spent most of his childhood in the house of a prosperous white family named Aarons, because the patriarch had asked his mother for one of her boys to help around the place and she gave up the darker one. In 1943 he enlisted at Camp Shelby and went to New Guinea, where he drove ammunition trucks and learned to box.

He was five foot eight and two hundred twenty pounds and built like a door. The Army rated his character excellent, discharged him honorably in July of 1944, and handed him three hundred dollars in mustering out pay.

He came home with it and built a logging business.

He bought land, put cattle on it and vegetables in it, married a woman named Elizabeth and raised four children. He became a man white men in Liberty did business with, which in that county was a tightrope people walked their whole lives.

He walked it for sixteen years. Then, on the twenty-fifth of September, 1961, he pulled his truck into a line at a cotton gin and it came to an end.

Ahead of him in that line was a dairy farmer named Herbert Lee, who had nine children and who was one of the first Black men in Amite County to try to put his name on a voter roll. Coming toward Lee across the lot was a white man named E. H. Hurst, a member of the Mississippi House of Representatives, with a .38 in his hand.

Hurst and Lee had played together as boys, a long time ago, and it did not appear to be on either man's mind.

Lee would not talk while the gun was out. Hurst let it drop, and Lee stepped down out of his truck with his hands empty and an unlit cigarette in his mouth, and Hurst brought the gun back up and fired once.

Louis Allen and about a dozen other men stood there and watched it happen.

They did not have to wait long for the reckoning. A coroner's jury was seated that same day, in a courtroom filled with white men who had brought their guns in with them.

Before it convened, the law got to the witnesses. Louis Allen was told what he was going to say, which was that Herbert Lee had come at a state legislator with a tire iron.

He said at first that he would not swear to something he had not seen.

Then he was told that if he did not, they would kill his entire family. He had a wife and four children about three miles up the road, and so Louis Allen stood up in that room and said he had seen a tire iron in a dead man's hand.

Five men said it. The jury took no time at all and found that Representative Hurst had defended himself, and Hurst walked out of the courthouse and drove home and was never charged with anything, ever.

That should have been the end of it. Louis Allen had done what the county required and he was free to go back to hauling timber.

It was not the end of it, and the reason why is the whole story.

His wife explained it years later, in a deposition she gave to the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party in the summer of 1964. If he had told a story on a living man, Elizabeth Allen said, he could go and ask that man to forgive him.

He could not ask a dead one. So, she said, his conscience was clipping him.

It clipped him for months. Then he found Bob Moses of SNCC and told him that if somebody could keep his family safe, he would go before a federal grand jury and let the hide go with the hair.

Those were his words. SNCC carried the message to the Justice Department, and the Justice Department sent back that there was no protection available.

And then, somehow, Liberty found out he had offered.

What happened to Louis Allen after that took two years and never once required a white man in that county to break a law any other white man would enforce. His timber customers quit him one by one, until he was driving into Louisiana to buy gas and hunting work in counties far enough off that nobody had heard about him.

In June of 1962 a deputy named Daniel Jones came to the house to arrest him for interfering with an officer. Hank was there and watched his father put his wrists out to be cuffed.

Louis asked if he could have his hat.

Jones said no. Louis asked, then, whether his boy could carry the hat out to him.

What Jones did next was hit him in the face with a flashlight hard enough to break his jaw.

Two months after that, with his jaw wired, Louis Allen walked into the courthouse in Liberty and tried to register to vote. There were gunshots outside and the power went out inside, and he did not get registered, and no Black person in Amite County had been permitted to since 1890.

In November of 1963 Jones arrested him again, for carrying a weapon and for writing a check that was overdrawn by two or three dollars.

His older son Tommie did not believe his father would come out of that jail alive. He told Hank they had better make sure the old man was actually locked up and stayed that way, and then the two boys took two old guns down to the jailhouse next to the courthouse in Liberty.

They stayed there all night. One brother stood by the outhouse across from the front door watching for anybody who came, and the other slept in the car, and then they traded.

They did that for about twenty nights, until the NAACP raised eight hundred dollars and bonded him out.

After that he stopped arguing about leaving. His brother Morris was in Milwaukee and would help him find work, and Louis told his family he was tired of being picked on, which is a small phrase for what had been done to him.

His parents were old and sick and living in a house on his land, and he would not go while they needed him. His mother died on Wednesday, January 22, 1964.

He set his departure for that Saturday.

On the Friday he drove over to see a former boss of his named Lloyd King and asked him for a letter he could show a man in Wisconsin. King wrote it out by hand and Louis folded it into his pocket.

It said that Lewis Allen was a good truck driver and could run a cat, that he had worked several years for the writer, and that the writer had been pleased with his work. King spelled his name wrong.

That was the last piece of paper Louis Allen ever carried, and his name was misspelled on it.

That same evening, before he drove off, his son held the gap open for him and followed him through and closed it behind them both.

"Whatever you do, son, you look out for your mom and your little sister," Louis told him.

"Daddy's gonna go up there, go to work. In about three weeks, I'll be sending for y'all."

Then Hank went to his party in Gloster, and his father went to get his letter, and a few hours later the boy stepped on his hand in the dark.

Sheriff Daniel Jones came out to the property with a doctor. Standing over the body, in front of the dead man's teenage son, he said he would see if he could find what caused the problem.

Then he went through Louis Allen's pockets.

He took out the wallet and went through the cash, and then he went through the cards, and he came to a small one that said Louis Allen was a member of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. He stopped there and told Hank he would need to keep the wallet overnight.

He brought it back the next day. The NAACP card was not in it.

That is the part to hold on to, because everything after it turns on that card.

The coroner's jury Jones assembled the next morning found that Louis Allen had been killed by an assailant or assailants unknown. Jones told reporters he had no idea why anyone would want the man dead, and floated to the FBI that it might have been trouble between Louis and his wife.

The Justice Department did send agents. For ten days they interviewed Elizabeth Allen, Lloyd King, Daniel Jones and others around Liberty.

Elizabeth told them her husband had not been involved in voter registration work.

Understand what she was doing. Her husband was in the ground, the sheriff who had broken his jaw was running the investigation, and she had children left in that house who could still be killed.

Hank had driven his father to NAACP meetings himself, out in the woods outside Liberty where Black men taught each other to read and write. He used to flick his headlights on and off before he pulled up, in case anybody was following.

The FBI wrote its report and closed the file. It concluded that the victim was not a registered voter, had never been active in voter registration work, and that there had been no voter registration activity in Amite County in the past two or three years.

All three statements were true, and the reason all three were true is the reason he was dead.

On the morning of Saturday, February 1, the Council of Federated Organizations was in the middle of a staff meeting in Hattiesburg. They had spent months arguing over a proposal to bring a large number of white northern college students into Mississippi that summer, and they were getting nowhere with it.

The meeting was interrupted by a phone call from Amite County.

Bob Moses had stayed mostly quiet through that argument. After the call he stopped being quiet, and afterward he said only that it had become clear they had to do something big enough to open the situation up.

They already knew what would open it, and that is the part that never makes the anniversary posts.

Herbert Lee had been killed by a sitting state legislator in front of a dozen witnesses and the country had not turned its head. Louis Allen had been killed at his own gate and the country had not turned its head.

So they built a summer out of that fact. Bring down white students from good families in New York and California, and when Mississippi did to those students what it had been doing to people like Louis Allen for ninety years, the cameras would come, and the federal government would follow the cameras.

Grown people sat in a room and decided to use their own country's racism as a lever, because nothing else had ever moved it.

Volunteers began arriving at a small women's college in Oxford, Ohio on June 14, somewhere between seven hundred and a thousand of them. On the lawns they were taught how to fall and cover their heads, while SNCC and CORE staff rolled up sleeves and showed them the scars.

Six days after the first group crossed into Mississippi, it worked.

James Chaney, a Black CORE worker from Meridian, drove out with Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner to look at a burned church in Neshoba County. A deputy arrested the three of them, held them, and turned them loose after dark.

Within days the President was involved, sailors were walking the swamps, and it was on every front page in America.

And while they dragged the rivers looking for two white men and one Black man, they kept bringing up people nobody had been looking for.

On July 12, in a channel of the Mississippi down near Natchez, the search brought up a body that was none of the three. The next day it brought up another.

They were Henry Hezekiah Dee and Charles Eddie Moore, both about nineteen, who had been hitchhiking outside Meadville on the second of May when Klansmen picked them up on the wrong assumption that they were organizers. Neither one had ever been in the movement, and they had been gone ten weeks, and no search had ever been sent out for them.

There was a fourteen-year-old boy, Herbert Oarsby, found in a CORE shirt. There were five more men who were never identified and never will be.

Once it was clear these were not the bodies the country was watching for, the reporters packed up.

Chaney, Goodman and Schwerner were found on August 4 under an earthen dam, forty-four days gone. Michael Schwerner's widow Rita was twenty-two years old, and she stood in front of the press and would not let them make it into something clean.

The killing of a Black man in Mississippi was not news, she told them. The alarm had been sounded only because her husband and Andrew Goodman were white.

She was not being bitter, she was reading the plan back to them out loud, and she had more right to say it than anybody standing there.

Measured against the thing it said it was doing, the summer failed. Around seventeen thousand Black Mississippians went to a courthouse that summer and filled out the form, and about sixteen hundred of them ended up on the rolls.

The rest of the ledger runs like this. One thousand and sixty-two arrests, eighty workers beaten, thirty-seven churches bombed or burned, thirty homes and businesses the same, four civil rights workers killed, and at least three local Black Mississippians killed for their part in it.

One column came out ahead. Around forty Freedom Schools opened, and more than three thousand children and grown folks came through them to study reading, civics, and their own history for the first time in their lives.

And on August 22 a sharecropper's daughter from Ruleville sat down in front of the Democratic Party's credentials committee in Atlantic City, gave her name, and then gave her home address out loud on national television.

Mississippi had written its laws specifically to make that information deadly. Fannie Lou Hamer said it into a microphone on purpose.

The President of the United States called an emergency press conference to pull the networks off her. They ran her that night anyway, in full, and the mail came in by the sack.

Louis Allen had been in the ground about seven months by then.

They buried him on a Monday morning at Star Hill Baptist Church, and Hank says the building could not hold half the people who came. That same evening Elizabeth put her son and her little girl Mary in a car and took them across the line into Louisiana, to relatives, because she did not believe the house was survivable anymore.

Hank was seventeen and there was no money. He hooked scrap iron out of the Mississippi River for eight dollars a day for six months, until his mother made him go back and finish his senior year on the grounds that his father would have wanted the diploma.

Almost exactly a year after the gate, he came home one evening and found her frightened. She had dreamed that men in Liberty were coming to kill him, and she told him he had to go north.

He left that same night, caught a train out of New Orleans, and rode it to Milwaukee.

Sit with that. The trip Louis Allen was packed for, the one he was going to send for his family in three weeks to join, was finally made by his son, one year later, running.

Nobody has ever been arrested for it. The FBI reopened the case in 2006 with Daniel Jones as its subject, and the Justice Department finally closed the file in May of 2015, under a heading that reads Daniel Jones, Deceased.

In 1988, Louis Allen's grandson Kevin heard that Jones was still alive and working at a hardware store in Liberty. He drove there, walked in past the barrel of ax handles by the door, and stood in front of the old sheriff.

"You thought you killed Louis Allen," Kevin told him, "but you multiplied him. There was one, now there are several."

Then he walked out and drove off, and he says Jones grabbed at his chest and did not say one word.

There is a boy in that family now, a great-grandson, who boxes. Before every fight he ties on a white bandana with two gloves printed on it and four words between them, which are RIP LOUIS ALLEN.

That is a family that has been printing his name on whatever it can find for sixty-two years, because a sheriff took the only card that had it on him and the United States government wrote down that he was nobody in particular.

So print it somewhere. Louis Allen, Herbert Lee, Henry Dee, Charles Moore, Herbert Oarsby, and the five men out of the river who were never given a name at all.

His stone is out on Old Compromise Road, and the silver paint on the letters has gone dull.

Louis Allen's story was almost buried inside a file number, a missing card, and a forgotten grave. I share stories like his because sometimes the first step toward justice is simply making sure people know the name.

I don’t normally do much advertising of my published books on my 2nd Mississippi page. I’ll occasionally mention them and offer a link. But I just had my self-publishing author’s “imprint” logo professionally redone and thought I’d share the story of how “Coonewah Creek Publishing” came to be. 

About Coonewah Creek Publishing

Why the name "Coonewah Creek" for my publishing imprint cover? Well, my great-grandfather fought for the 2nd Mississippi Infantry Regiment. His company was Company H...the Coonewah Rifles (often misspelled "Coonwah"). The name came from a creek in Pontotoc County, Mississippi where he was from. The name itself was apparently derived from the Chickasaw Native American tribe's language that populated the area before their forced removal to what is now Oklahoma. The most widely accepted (but disputed) translation is that in the Chickasaw language, "Coonewah" literally means "ripe polecat" or equivalently "smelly skunk." Thus the skunk logo. The word itself is pronounced either "KOO-nuh-wah" or "KOO-nee-wah." Personally, I prefer the first pronunciation.

🕊️ The Plight of the Deceased Father
Narada explained that during his travels through Yamaloka, he encountered King Indrasena’s deceased father. Because of an incomplete spiritual duty and a few unatoned mistakes committed in his previous life, the late king’s soul was stuck in Yama’s custody and was unable to attain Moksha (liberation).
Narada delivered the father's exact message to the king: "O my noble son, please perform the Indira Ekadashi Vrat during the dark fortnight of the month of Ashwin. If you formally dedicate the spiritual fruits and merits of this single fast to me, my soul will be instantly freed from Yamaloka and I will be allowed to ascend to the heavenly realms".

📜 The Divine Method Prescribed by Narada
Distressed by his father's condition, King Indrasena pleaded with Narada Muni to teach him the exact rules to perform this fast perfectly. Narada Muni instructed him as follows:
On Dashami (The 10th Day): Cleanse yourself thoroughly in the morning. In the afternoon, perform the mandatory Shradh rituals and offer food to your ancestors out of deep devotion. Eat only one simple, pure satvik meal at night and maintain complete celibacy.
On Ekadashi (The 11th Day): Wake up early, take a holy bath, and take a solemn vow (Sankalpa) to fast completely for the day to please Lord Vishnu. At noon, worship the Shaligram form of Lord Sri Vishnu with incense, flowers, and lamps. Perform Tarpan (water offerings) for your forefathers, feed qualified saints/Brahmins, and offer the ritual food (Pindas) to a holy cow. Stay awake all night chanting the glories of Lord Hari.
On Dwadashi (The 12th Day): Wake up early, perform a final morning prayer to Lord Sri Vishnu, feed the needy and your relatives, and break the fast in silent gratitude.
After imparting this sacred knowledge, Sage Narada disappeared into the heavens.

✨ Liberation and Divine Blessings
King Indrasena, alongside his family and royal subjects, followed every instruction of the Devarishi with pristine devotion.
As the king successfully completed the fast and broke it on Dwadashi, a miraculous sight unfolded. Flowers rained down from the open sky. The massive spiritual merit generated by Indrasena’s fast instantly broke the ancestral chains of his father. The father's soul received a completely radiant, spiritual body, and he safely ascended to Vaikuntha (the heavenly supreme abode of Lord Sri Vishnu) on the back of Garuda.
King Indrasena went on to rule his kingdom smoothly for many more years, eventually handing the throne over to his son before peacefully ascending to heaven himself.

Lord Sri Krishna concluded the narration by telling King Yudhishthira that anyone who strictly observes the Indira Ekadashi Vrat cleanses their entire lineage, frees their ancestors from lower realms, and ultimately achieves salvation. Even simply reading or hearing this sacred Vrat Katha bestows a spiritual benefit equivalent to performing a horse sacrifice (Ashvamedha Yajna).

Question 3 would replace Massachusetts party primaries with a single “all-party” or top-two primary. Every candidate would appear on one ballot. Only the top two vote-getters would advance to November, even if they belong to the same party.This proposed change is a solution looking for a problem that does not exist—especially for unenrolled voters.
● Unenrolled voters already have the right to participate in Massachusetts primaries. They simply choose a Democratic or Republican ballot on primary day.
● They can vote in the race that matters most in their community without joining a party.
● Voters could be disenfranchised negatively impacting turnout and distorting the will of the people on ballot questions.
● Question 3 does not give unenrolled voters a new right. It takes away a system they already use and understand.
The proposed top-two system would weaken parties and shrink real choice.
● Parties exist so voters can choose between distinct political philosophies. Question 3 removes their ability to nominate their own candidates to run in the general election.
● In a heavily partisan state, the two highest finishers would often both be of one party. Third party candidates and many independents would be shut out of the general election—the contest that draws the most voters.
● November ballots would offer less ideological diversity when turnout and attention are highest.

Rust Daily Digest — October 5, 2026

I'll pull the latest Rust-related coverage from the past day and condense the top stories with a takeaway and link each. Most hits so far are the October 1 release and the game. I'm narrowing to language and tooling items from the last day. A strict 24-hour window (4–5 October 2026) does not contain ten independent Rust project announcements. The list below is the highest-signal language and toolchain coverage from that window, with the 1 October stable release included because it is still the item driving most discussion. Facepunch game “Rust” items are excluded.

Ubuntu 26.10 beta pushes Rust further into the base system. The Register’s 5 October write-up covers the “Stonking Stingray” beta (final target 15 October): coreutils are fully on uutils, and stock OpenPGP moves to Rust-based Sequoia-PGP.
Takeaway: Canonical’s “oxidization” now covers both everyday Unix tools and the default OpenPGP stack, not only a partial coreutils swap.
https://t.co/wy8WpeWrFd

Microsoft’s internal Tier-1 status is still being reported as fresh news. IT-Connect (5 October) restates the RustConf / Rust Foundation guest post: Rust sits with C++, C#, and TypeScript for internal Microsoft development, backed by the closed rustc_codegen_utc backend into the MSVC UTC code generator.
Takeaway: This is an internal support label, not a Rust project platform tier; the substance is shared codegen with C++, already used by 100+ Microsoft repos.
https://t.co/lmnzM5XnUD

Headstart pipelines crate builds on early metadata. Coverage on 4–5 October describes six rustc patches and three Cargo patches that start dependents once a dependency’s interface is checked, before function bodies finish. Clean cargo check was up to 54% faster on 16 cores (rust-analyzer, Zed, Bevy, and others); none of the measured projects slowed down.
Takeaway: Downstream crates only need .rmeta interfaces, so waiting on body checking is idle time that can be overlapped.
https://t.co/bXaptjTkPO

Follow-up on how the early-metadata swap works. A 5 October technical note walks through the second metadata file, the abandoned 2019 attempt, and the core-count assumption behind the speedup (about 24% on 4 cores versus 54% on 16).
Takeaway: Gains depend on spare cores; headstart parallelizes across crates, while -Zthreads parallelizes inside one crate.
https://t.co/xlkOjdas4t

CPython sketches an optional Rust path, not a hard requirement. Slashdot (4 October) reports the Python Language Summit proposal: optional Rust in 3.16 (October 2027), with zlib via zlib-rs as the first module, and Rust required to build CPython no earlier than 3.18 (2029).
Takeaway: The near-term bet is a faster, optional zlib that would speed packaging installs, with C kept as the fallback.
https://t.co/UCfK7PwZl2

Google agents are being used on large C/C++-to-Rust ports. The 4 October Rust Trends issue highlights Gemini 4 Argon migrations from libraries such as re2 and libgav1 up to more than 800,000 lines in the Fuchsia Zircon kernel. The libgav1 case replaced about 32,000 lines of SIMD with safe Rust the compiler vectorizes, reported at 2.7× the prior Rust port.
Takeaway: Google is treating the rewrite as a reviewed, scaled program; output still goes through audit, emulation, and human review.
https://t.co/XZKn8AiRCq

Same digest: rustc wall time down 4.57% over two months. Nicholas Nethercote’s 29 July–28 September compiler performance note, summarized 4 October, shows a 4.57% mean wall-time drop and improvement on 555 of 629 measurements. LLVM 23 alone was about 1.2%; Clippy PGO reached about 18% on Clippy benchmarks.
Takeaway: The speedup is a stack of small wins, not one flag; Polonius Alpha and the next trait solver remain nightly work with known regressions.
https://t.co/XZKn8AiRCq

Rust 1.99.0 remains the dominant official item (1 October). Stable now allows defining extern "C" and extern "C-unwind" variadic functions in Rust via VaList, settles size and alignment queries on raw pointers (including unsized types), and stabilizes APIs such as Vec::into_parts / from_parts, VecDeque::retain_back, and std::fs::set_times.
Takeaway: FFI authors can implement C-style varargs in Rust instead of only calling them. Update with rustup update stable.
https://t.co/wOCpE5A3Jp

Takeaway: Kernel and systems readers get the same headline without the full release-blog walkthrough.

text:
Russell L. Estes
 ·
Tuscaloosa, Alabama. An apartment complex. There I was watching a bunch of professional shingle slingers and highly trained swear-word inventors put in an honest day’s work. Well… “honest” might be stretching it a little.
The hammers were keeping rhythm with a mariachi band coming through somebody’s speaker, and every now and then somebody would holler something that probably wasn’t in the official roofing manual.
That’s where I met him. The kid was getting off the school bus near where we were working. He stopped for a minute and looked up at my guys. I couldn’t tell if he was admiring the craftsmanship or just trying to figure out how the stayed on the roof while line dancing.
But I noticed something. He never smiled.
He lived in the building we were working on, and when he asked if it was okay for him to walk through the breezeway, I got a good look at his eyes. Glossy. Red. Looked like the dam was about to give way.
“You good, buddy?” I asked.
“Don’t matter,” he said. “Nobody cares anyway.”
Well, I’ve never been accused of being particularly good at minding my own business, so I answered pretty quickly.
“I do. And I’d bet a bunch more folks do too.”
We only talked for a minute or so. He explained his situation. He’d finally worked up the courage to ask a pretty little girl on the bus to be his girlfriend. She said no. Then she laughed.
Now, anybody who has ever been twelve years old—or remembers being twelve years old—knows there are few things more devastating than having your heart handed back to you by somebody who thinks it’s funny.
But that wasn’t all…
He told me his family didn’t have the money to give him what some of the other kids had. They couldn’t take him everywhere the other kids went. They didn’t have all the things other families had. And somehow, in his young mind, that made him different. Less. Not as important or cool as the kids who had more.
I didn’t have much to offer. My advice is worth about as much as a pair of flip flops is to Lieutenant Dan. But I didn’t give him one of my “God Is Bigger” bracelets.
I told him to hang in there. I told him things would get better. And I meant every word.
But as he walked away, I knew something. Sometimes a five-minute conversation can plant a seed, but it can’t grow the whole garden. I wished I could do more.
Then I remembered a kid I once knew. He was about the same age. That kid knew what it was like to watch other children go places he couldn’t go. He knew what it was like to see somebody wearing something new while he was wearing something that had already belonged to somebody else.
Most of his shoes were hand-me-downs. He didn’t have fancy clothes. He didn’t have a closet full of options. But he had something a whole lot more valuable. He knew he was loved. He had friends. And he was happy.
One morning, picture day rolled around at school. Now, this particular kid had a serious problem. His hair needed cutting. Bad. His mama usually cut his hair herself, which meant there was always a certain amount of prayer involved in the process. Unfortunately, she hadn’t gotten around to it before picture day.
His bangs had gotten so long he could barely see through them. So this brilliant young fella did what any responsible child would do. He found a pair of dull scissors… and cut his own hair.
I use the word “cut” loosely. One side was shorter than the other. Much shorter. It looked less like a haircut and more like two barber shops had gotten into an argument and quit halfway through.
But the hair wasn’t even his biggest problem. He didn’t have anything “cool” to wear for picture day. So he went digging through his brother’s closet and found a denim button-up shirt. It was way too big. I mean, REALLY too big. He looked like somebody had put a ten-year-old inside a shirt designed for a grown man and said, “That’ll do.”
And you know what? It did. He went to school anyway. The other kids noticed the shirt. They noticed the crooked haircut. They noticed the bangs that looked like they’d been trimmed by a squirrel with commitment issues.
But something else happened that day. At recess, he was picked first for the kickball team. And that boy could kick a ball. He sent one flying farther than anybody expected.
Everybody yelled. They high-fived the kid. Everybody had a good time. And by the end of the day, that crooked haircut didn’t matter quite as much as it had that morning.
Because that kid eventually learned something. Life doesn’t always give you what you want. Sometimes it gives you hand-me-down shoes. Sometimes it gives you an oversized shirt. Sometimes it gives you a haircut that should probably be entered into evidence. And sometimes it gives you a girl on the school bus who says no and then laughs about it.
But none of those things get to decide your worth. That kid learned that having less doesn’t mean you are less. In fact, sometimes having less teaches you to appreciate more.
You learn to appreciate a good friend. A mama who does the best she can with what she has. You learn that some of the best memories don’t require a credit card. And eventually, you realize something the world is always trying to make us forget: The most important things in life aren’t for sale.
You can’t buy somebody who truly loves you. You can’t purchase a loyal friend. You can’t put a price tag on peace. And you sure can’t swipe a credit card for a childhood full of good memories.
So, kid… Hang in there. That girl on the bus may have told you no.
But one day you might have a wife so beautiful that people will question her eyesight.
You’ll have friends you can count on.
You’ll have people who love you for who you are and not for what you own.
And maybe, just maybe, you’ll look back one day and realize that the things you thought made you different were actually preparing you for the life God had planned all along.
Because sometimes the people who grow up with the least learn how to appreciate the most. And sometimes the kid who doesn’t get to go everywhere learns to enjoy wherever he is. And sometimes the kid who doesn’t have the newest clothes ends up wearing a life that fits him better than anything money could buy.
So keep going, buddy. God is bigger.
Bigger than the voice in your head telling you that you aren’t enough.
You are.
And one more thing…
On picture day, don’t cut your own hair…
WAIT FOR YOUR MAMA.
Trust me.
